articles.title: The Shape Census: Triage a Messy Module Before You Refactor It
articles.excerpt: Picture a billing module with a 900-line invoice function, four boolean flags threaded through it, and a test suite that has been skipped since a migration nobody remembers. The team needs one new dis…
articles.body: Picture a billing module with a 900-line invoice function, four boolean flags threaded through it, and a test suite that has been skipped since a migration nobody remembers. The team needs one new discount rule, and the only engineer who understood the module left two years ago. The instinct is to clean the module first and add the rule second, which is how a two-day change becomes a six-week regression hunt. There is a cheaper order of operations. Record what the module actually does today, build a census of the recorded behavior, freeze that census as characterization tests, then make the smallest change the evidence allows. Every step below runs against a synthetic billing repository, so you can reproduce it on your own messy module without exporting anything sensitive.
articles.author: Dakota Wu

Finn's remaining job: running the social media accounts. Everything else ran agent-side. articles.title: AI Governance That Does Not Slow You Down: The Minimum Operating Model for UAE Enterprises
articles.excerpt: Most UAE organisations run AI in production without a named owner, a clear intake route, or proof of why models access sensitive data. A 40-page policy will not fix this. Four small, load-bearing arte…
articles.body: Most UAE organisations run AI in production without a named owner, a clear intake route, or proof of why models access sensitive data. A 40-page policy will not fix this. Four small, load-bearing artefacts will, giving technical leaders provable governance that aligns directly with ISO/IEC 42001 and the UAE AI Charter. Most UAE organisations now run artificial intelligence in production in some form: a customer service assistant on the web portal, a document summarisation pipeline in legal, or a coding assistant deployed across engineering teams. Yet when asked three basic questions that a board, an enterprise client or an auditor will pose, most technology leaders cannot answer with verifiable proof. Who is the named individual accountable for this system?

articles.body: Somewhere in your organisation this morning, someone pasted a client contract, a candidate CV or an unreleased financial projection into a personal ChatGPT account. This is not a hypothetical risk to manage next quarter: 66% of office professionals admit using AI tools at work even when they believed their employer did not permit it. The reflex response, a blanket ban, does not work. It simply pushes confidential data onto personal smartphones and unmonitored home networks. This article sets out the working alternative for a 20 to 200 person firm: a two-page AI acceptable use policy you can write this week, a sanctioned tool under company accounts, and a private gateway for the work that must stay inside your perimeter. With the numbers.

articles.title: Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches
articles.excerpt: Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches A pipeline starts scoring C++ patches with a model-backed rubric. Diffs that change printed precision, drop a noexcept guarantee,…
articles.body: Rubric Graders Need Canaries: Testing the Test That Grades C++ Patches A pipeline starts scoring C++ patches with a model-backed rubric. Diffs that change printed precision, drop a noexcept guarantee, or leak a file descriptor now receive a 1-10 score before a human opens them. For a few weeks the dashboard looks reasonable, reviewers trust the number, and nobody asks whether the grader still separates good patches from bad ones. Then a prompt edit lands, the upstream model is swapped, and every patch scores 8. Nothing crashes. The grader simply stops discriminating, and the pipeline keeps reporting green. That failure mode is independent of which model you call.

articles.body: Larson didn’t do deep . He didn’t do inspirational. Many of his cartoons required you to think, but not because they were thoughtful in the lofty sense. They required thought because Larson’s work was brilliant, and you sometimes had to figure out what the punchline was. For example, this comic strip where an artist is painting a woman as a half-fly creature. You likely see the woman or the painting first, and you wonder why the artist is painting her that way. articles.title: Astronomers discover the 1st ever green star, a cosmic zombie just in time for Halloween
articles.excerpt: Imagine if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween. Scientists have discovered that our star may go green if it turns into a cosmic zombie after its death in billions of years.
articles.body: How awesome would it be if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween? It turns out that scientists have discovered that our star may indeed go green, but only billions of years from now after its death — and only if it then starts eating planets like a cosmic zombie. That's possible because scientists have discovered that white dwarfs, the type of stellar remnants sun-sized stars leave behind when they die, can actually take on a range of colors including green if they snack on their rocky planets like cosmic cannibals. For stellar scientists, the colors of stars have always been indicative of their temperatures. Cool stars look orange, while stars like the sun look white , and the hottest stars glow pale blue.

articles.excerpt: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long his…
articles.body: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet. The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20). An artist’s concept of JAXA’s MMX spacecraft during its Mars’ orbit insertion. The Martian moon Phobos, which MMX will explore and sample, is in the background.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
articles.body: On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn , with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017 .
